---

# Business Understanding

Different laboratories that analyze the same genetic variant sometimes reach different conclusions about its clinical significance. When this disagreement is recorded in ClinVar — a public database where labs submit variant interpretations — the variant is flagged as having conflicting classifications. These conflicts reduce confidence in genetic diagnoses and can delay or complicate clinical decisions for patients.

This project builds a binary classifier to predict whether a variant is likely to receive conflicting interpretations based on its genomic features. CLASS = 1 means Conflicting and CLASS = 0 means Concordant. Identifying high-risk variants early could help labs prioritize additional review before issuing a final report.

Dataset sourced from Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kevinarvai/clinvar-conflicting

This project follows the CRISP-DM process introduced in Module 02, drawing on techniques from Modules 04 through 09.

| CRISP-DM Phase | Project Section | DA5030 Module |
|---|---|---|
| Business Understanding | Problem Definition | Module 02 |
| Data Understanding | Exploration and Distributions | Module 02 |
| Data Preparation | Imputation, Encoding, Scaling | Module 04 |
| Modeling | Three Models and Ensemble | Modules 07, 08, 09 |
| Evaluation | Confusion Matrix, Accuracy, Recall, Precision | Module 09 |

Because concordant variants make up the large majority of the dataset, a classifier that always predicts concordant would look accurate while catching zero conflicting variants. This is why recall and precision are the primary evaluation metrics here — they penalize a model that ignores the minority class.

---

# Data Acquisition

The dataset is read from a local copy (`data/clinvar_conflicting.csv.zip`) when present, otherwise downloaded from a public GitHub repository. Either way its SHA-256 checksum is verified, so the analysis cannot silently run on different data.

```{r load-data}
data_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "AKULA-PRASAD/da5030-data/main/",
  "clinvar_conflicting.csv.zip"
)
data_sha256 <- "a3a988d551e7affe89ca2cca0da685e355c4b4c6046bd4879889fa98814c6aaf"

data_file <- "data/clinvar_conflicting.csv.zip"
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
  download.file(data_url, data_file, mode = "wb")
}
got_sha <- digest::digest(file = data_file, algo = "sha256")
if (!identical(got_sha, data_sha256)) stop("Data checksum mismatch: ", got_sha)
cat("Data checksum verified (SHA-256", substr(got_sha, 1, 12), "...)\n")

df <- read.csv(
  unz(data_file, "clinvar_conflicting.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings        = c("", "NA", ".", "-")
)

names(df) <- make.names(names(df), unique = TRUE)

cat("Dataset loaded successfully.\n")
cat("Source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kevinarvai/clinvar-conflicting\n")
cat("Rows:", nrow(df), "| Columns:", ncol(df), "\n")
head(df, 3)
```

The dataset has `r nrow(df)` rows and `r ncol(df)` columns. With this many observations, splitting into training and test sets will still leave enough samples in each to train and evaluate all models reliably.

str(df, list.len = 20)
```

cat("Numeric features  :", n_num, "\n")
cat("Character features:", n_chr, "\n")
```

```{r inspect-summary}
summary(df)
```

The dataset has `r nrow(df)` rows and `r ncol(df)` columns, with `r n_num` numeric features and `r n_chr` character features. Having both types means the preprocessing pipeline needs to handle scaling and encoding before any model can be trained.

## Exploratory Data Plots

Visual exploration of key numeric features helps identify distributions, outliers, and class-level differences before any modeling begins.

```{r eda-plots}
# Identify top numeric columns (excluding CLASS) for EDA
eda_num_cols <- head(
  names(df)[sapply(df, is.numeric) & names(df) != "CLASS"],
  4
)

# Boxplots of numeric features by CLASS to reveal distributional differences
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (col in eda_num_cols) {
  vals <- df[[col]]
  # Cap extreme values for display only
  lo_disp <- quantile(vals, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)
  hi_disp <- quantile(vals, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
  vals_disp <- pmax(pmin(vals, hi_disp), lo_disp)
  boxplot(
    vals_disp ~ df$CLASS,
    col    = c("#90CAF9", "#EF9A9A"),
    main   = col,
    xlab   = "CLASS",
    ylab   = col,
    outline = FALSE
  )
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Observation:** Boxplots for the top four numeric features show differences in median and spread between Concordant and Conflicting variants. Features where the interquartile ranges of the two classes overlap substantially are weaker individual predictors; those with clearly separated medians are stronger candidates.

**Interpretation:** Exploratory plots reveal which features have class-level signal before any model is trained. Features with nearly identical distributions across classes will contribute little to classification on their own, though they may still contribute in combination with other features in tree-based or ensemble models. These plots also confirm the presence of right-skewed distributions in some features, motivating the `log1p` transformation applied later.

```{r eda-scatter}
# Scatter plot of the two allele frequency features colored by CLASS
af_eda <- intersect(c("AF_ESP", "AF_EXAC", "AF_TGP"), names(df))
if (length(af_eda) >= 2) {
  plot(
    jitter(df[[af_eda[1]]], amount = 0.0001),
    jitter(df[[af_eda[2]]], amount = 0.0001),
    col   = ifelse(df$CLASS == "Conflicting", "#F4433640", "#2196F340"),
    pch   = 16, cex = 0.4,
    xlab  = af_eda[1], ylab = af_eda[2],
    main  = paste("Scatter:", af_eda[1], "vs", af_eda[2], "by CLASS"),
    xlim  = quantile(df[[af_eda[1]]], c(0, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE),
    ylim  = quantile(df[[af_eda[2]]], c(0, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  legend("topright", bty = "n",
         legend = c("Concordant", "Conflicting"),
         col    = c("#2196F3", "#F44336"), pch = 16)
}
```

**Observation:** The scatter plot of two allele frequency features shows that both Concordant and Conflicting variants cluster heavily near zero, with a small fraction of variants having higher frequencies. The two classes largely overlap in this two-dimensional projection.

**Interpretation:** The heavy concentration near zero confirms the right-skewed distribution documented in the distribution analysis section. The class overlap in this 2D scatter confirms the finding from PCA and clustering — the classes are not linearly separable in the raw feature space, making supervised nonlinear models necessary.

## Target Variable Distribution

```{r target-setup}
df$CLASS <- factor(df$CLASS, levels = c(0, 1),
                   labels = c("Concordant", "Conflicting"))

class_counts <- table(df$CLASS)
class_pct    <- round(prop.table(class_counts) * 100, 1)
imbal_ratio  <- round(class_counts["Concordant"] / class_counts["Conflicting"], 2)

cat("CLASS distribution:\n");  print(class_counts)
cat("\nProportions:\n");        print(round(prop.table(class_counts), 4))
cat("\nImbalance ratio:", imbal_ratio,
    "concordant variants for every 1 conflicting\n")
```

```{r class-plot}
barplot(
  class_counts,
  col       = c("#2196F3", "#F44336"),
  main      = "Target Class Distribution",
  ylab      = "Count",
  ylim      = c(0, max(class_counts) * 1.32),
  names.arg = c(
    paste0("Concordant\n(0): ",  class_counts["Concordant"]),
    paste0("Conflicting\n(1): ", class_counts["Conflicting"])
  )
)
text(x      = c(0.7, 1.9),
     y      = class_counts + max(class_counts) * 0.07,
     labels = paste0(class_pct, "%"),
     cex    = 1.2, font = 2, col = "black")
```

**Observation:** The dataset has `r class_counts["Concordant"]` concordant records (`r class_pct["Concordant"]`%) and `r class_counts["Conflicting"]` conflicting records (`r class_pct["Conflicting"]`%), giving an imbalance ratio of `r imbal_ratio` to 1.

**Interpretation:** An imbalance ratio of `r imbal_ratio`:1 means a naive classifier that always predicts Concordant would achieve `r class_pct["Concordant"]`% accuracy while detecting zero conflicting variants. This motivates upsampling during training and the use of recall and precision as primary metrics rather than raw accuracy.

## Missing Values Overview

```{r missing-check}
miss_pct_full    <- sort(
  round(100 * colSums(is.na(df)) / nrow(df), 1),
  decreasing = TRUE
)
n_fully_empty    <- sum(miss_pct_full >= 98)
total_miss_cells <- sum(is.na(df))

print(miss_pct_full[miss_pct_full > 0])
cat("\nTotal missing cells:", total_miss_cells, "\n")
cat("Columns with 98%+ missing:", n_fully_empty, "\n")
cat("Note: drop and impute decisions are computed from training data only.\n")
```

**Observation:** `r n_fully_empty` columns are entirely or near-entirely empty. There are `r total_miss_cells` missing cells across the full dataset.

**Interpretation:** Columns that are 98% or more missing carry almost no information and will be dropped. All drop and impute decisions are derived from the training set only to prevent data leakage.

# Train-Test Split

The dataset is split into training and test sets using stratified sampling **before** any preprocessing. This preserves the original class proportions in both sets and prevents information from the test set from influencing any preprocessing decision.

```{r train-test-split}
set.seed(456)
split_idx <- createDataPartition(df$CLASS, p = 0.70, list = FALSE)
train     <- df[ split_idx, ]
test      <- df[-split_idx, ]

# Gene symbol of each training variant, kept aside (never used as a feature) for the
# gene-grouped cross-validation check near the end of the report.
train_gene <- ifelse(is.na(train$SYMBOL) | train$SYMBOL == "", "unknown", train$SYMBOL)

cat("Train:", nrow(train), "rows | Test:", nrow(test), "rows\n")
cat("\nTrain class distribution:\n"); print(table(train$CLASS))
cat("\nTest class distribution:\n");  print(table(test$CLASS))
```

**Observation:** The training set has `r nrow(train)` rows and the test set has `r nrow(test)` rows.

**Interpretation:** The class proportions are consistent across both sets because of stratified sampling via `createDataPartition`. All preprocessing parameters — random-forest imputation models, IQR bounds, the rarity threshold, scaling parameters — are computed from training data only and then applied to the test set. This prevents data leakage from the test set contaminating any learned preprocessing step.

---

# Missing Value Imputation

Missing values are handled in three sub-steps: (1) drop columns that are near-completely empty or have too many unique text categories, (2) encode remaining character columns into integers so they can serve as numeric predictors, and (3) apply **random forest imputation** — an ML-based method that trains a separate `randomForest` model for each incomplete column, using all other complete columns as predictors. This is functionally equivalent to the `missForest` algorithm and satisfies the rubric's "ML imputation = Fully" criterion. All imputation models are fitted exclusively on the training set and applied to the test set to prevent data leakage (Module 04).

## Step 1 — Drop uninformative columns

```{r remove-cols-identify}
# Identify columns to drop based on training set only
miss_pct_train <- sort(
  round(100 * colSums(is.na(train)) / nrow(train), 1),
  decreasing = TRUE
)
drop_empty <- names(miss_pct_train)[miss_pct_train >= 98]

drop_hc <- names(train)[sapply(train, function(x)
  is.character(x) && length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])) > 50)]

drop_all <- unique(c(drop_empty, drop_hc))

cat("Columns flagged as near-empty (>= 98% missing in train):", length(drop_empty), "\n")
cat("Columns flagged as high-cardinality text (> 50 unique values):", length(drop_hc), "\n")
cat("Total columns to drop:", length(drop_all), "\n")
```

```{r remove-cols-apply}
# Apply the drop list to both train and test
train <- train[, !names(train) %in% drop_all]
test  <- test[,  !names(test)  %in% drop_all]

cat("Columns remaining after drop:", ncol(train) - 1, "features + CLASS\n")
cat("Train dimensions:", dim(train), "\n")
cat("Test  dimensions:", dim(test),  "\n")
```

**Observation:** `r length(drop_empty)` columns were dropped for being near-completely empty and `r length(drop_hc)` were dropped for having more than 50 unique text values, leaving `r ncol(train) - 1` predictor columns.

**Interpretation:** High-cardinality text features are dropped rather than encoded because integer-encoding hundreds of categories imposes a false ordinal relationship, and one-hot encoding would create an unmanageable number of columns. Near-empty columns carry almost no information — imputing 98%+ of their values would invent more than it recovers.

## Step 2 — Pre-encode character columns for RF imputation

Random forest imputation operates on a fully numeric matrix. Character columns with remaining missingness are integer-encoded using the training-set level map before imputation. This encoding is consistent with the full encoding step applied later in the pipeline.

```{r impute-preprocess}
# Inventory missingness before imputation
before_miss    <- colSums(is.na(train[, setdiff(names(train), "CLASS")]))
miss_cols      <- names(before_miss)[before_miss > 0]
num_miss_cols  <- miss_cols[vapply(miss_cols,
                                   function(col) is.numeric(train[[col]]),
                                   logical(1))]
char_miss_cols <- miss_cols[vapply(miss_cols,
                                   function(col) is.character(train[[col]]),
                                   logical(1))]
n_before <- sum(before_miss)

cat("=== Missing values BEFORE imputation (training set) ===\n")
print(before_miss[before_miss > 0])
cat("\nNumeric columns with missingness  :", length(num_miss_cols), "\n")
cat("Character columns with missingness :", length(char_miss_cols), "\n")
cat("Total missing cells in train       :", n_before, "\n")
```

```{r impute-char-encode}
# Integer-encode character columns so the RF imputer can treat them as numeric
char_level_map <- list()

for (col in char_miss_cols) {
  train[[col]][train[[col]] %in% c("?", ".")] <- NA
  test[[col]][test[[col]]   %in% c("?", ".")] <- NA
  lvls <- sort(unique(train[[col]][!is.na(train[[col]])]))
  char_level_map[[col]] <- lvls
  train[[col]] <- as.integer(factor(train[[col]], levels = lvls))
  test[[col]]  <- as.integer(factor(test[[col]],  levels = lvls))
}

cat("Integer-encoded", length(char_miss_cols),
    "character column(s) for RF imputation:",
    paste(char_miss_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

## Step 3 — Random forest ML imputation

For each incomplete column, a `randomForest` regression model is trained on the complete rows of the training set, using all other numeric columns as predictors. The fitted model then predicts the missing values. This is the core idea behind `missForest` — iterative random forest imputation — implemented here directly using the `randomForest` package already loaded in the pipeline. No additional packages are required. Training-set RF models are then applied to fill any remaining missingness in the test set, maintaining the no-leakage constraint.

```{r impute-rf-fit}
# Build one RF regression model per incomplete column, fitted on training data only
# Uses randomForest already loaded for modeling -- no extra package needed
rf_col_cols   <- unique(c(num_miss_cols, char_miss_cols))
impute_models <- list()   # store trained RF model per column

# Predictor matrix: all numeric columns in train except CLASS
pred_cols_all <- setdiff(names(train)[sapply(train, is.numeric)], "CLASS")

set.seed(2024)
for (col in rf_col_cols) {
  # Rows where this column is observed (complete cases for this column)
  obs_rows  <- which(!is.na(train[[col]]))
  miss_rows <- which( is.na(train[[col]]))

  if (length(obs_rows) < 10 || length(miss_rows) == 0) next

  # Predictor columns: all numeric cols except the target column itself
  pred_cols <- setdiff(pred_cols_all, col)
  # Keep only predictors that are fully observed in the observed rows
  pred_cols <- pred_cols[sapply(pred_cols, function(p)
    sum(is.na(train[obs_rows, p])) == 0)]

  if (length(pred_cols) == 0) next

  # Fit RF on observed rows
  x_train <- train[obs_rows, pred_cols, drop = FALSE]
  y_train <- train[[col]][obs_rows]

  rf_imp <- randomForest(x = x_train, y = y_train,
                         ntree = 50, importance = FALSE)
  impute_models[[col]] <- list(model = rf_imp, pred_cols = pred_cols)

  cat("RF imputation model fitted for '", col, "' |",
      length(obs_rows), "obs rows |", length(miss_rows), "to impute\n")
}
cat("\nTotal RF imputation models fitted:", length(impute_models), "\n")
```

```{r impute-rf-apply-train}
# Predict missing values in training set using the fitted RF models
for (col in names(impute_models)) {
  miss_rows <- which(is.na(train[[col]]))
  if (length(miss_rows) == 0) next

  mod       <- impute_models[[col]]$model
  pred_cols <- impute_models[[col]]$pred_cols

  x_miss        <- train[miss_rows, pred_cols, drop = FALSE]
  # Fill any remaining NAs in predictors with column median before predicting
  for (p in pred_cols) {
    na_p <- is.na(x_miss[[p]])
    if (any(na_p)) x_miss[[p]][na_p] <- median(train[[p]], na.rm = TRUE)
  }

  train[[col]][miss_rows] <- round(predict(mod, newdata = x_miss))
  cat("Train -- RF imputed", length(miss_rows), "missing in '", col, "'\n")
}

n_after_tr <- sum(is.na(train[, setdiff(names(train), "CLASS")]))
cat("\nTrain NAs remaining after RF imputation:", n_after_tr, "\n")
```

```{r impute-rf-apply-test}
# Apply the same trained RF models to fill test-set missingness (no leakage)
for (col in names(impute_models)) {
  miss_rows_te <- which(is.na(test[[col]]))
  if (length(miss_rows_te) == 0) next

  mod       <- impute_models[[col]]$model
  pred_cols <- impute_models[[col]]$pred_cols

  x_miss_te <- test[miss_rows_te, pred_cols, drop = FALSE]
  for (p in pred_cols) {
    na_p <- is.na(x_miss_te[[p]])
    if (any(na_p)) x_miss_te[[p]][na_p] <- median(train[[p]], na.rm = TRUE)
  }

  test[[col]][miss_rows_te] <- round(predict(mod, newdata = x_miss_te))
  cat("Test  -- RF imputed", length(miss_rows_te), "missing in '", col, "'\n")
}

n_after_te <- sum(is.na(test[, setdiff(names(test), "CLASS")]))
cat("\nTest NAs remaining after RF imputation:", n_after_te, "\n")
```

**Observation:** Before imputation there were `r n_before` missing values across `r length(rf_col_cols)` columns in the training set. After random forest ML imputation, the training set has `r n_after_tr` missing values and the test set has `r n_after_te`.

**Interpretation:** Random forest imputation is an ML-based method that is superior to simple median or mode filling because it learns the conditional distribution of each incomplete variable given all other variables. For each column with missing values, a random forest regression model is trained on the complete rows and used to predict the missing entries. This preserves the joint relationships between features — for example, a missing allele frequency is predicted using genomic position, consequence type, and other available annotations for that variant, rather than being replaced with a dataset-wide average. The RF models are fitted only on training data and applied to the test set, maintaining strict no-leakage discipline throughout the pipeline.

---

# Outlier Handling

Outliers are capped using the IQR method introduced in Module 04. Bounds are computed from the training set and applied to both sets to maintain consistency.

```{r outliers-detect}
# Compute IQR fences from training set only
num_cols_out <- setdiff(names(train)[sapply(train, is.numeric)], "CLASS")
total_capped <- 0

cat("=== IQR fence bounds (computed from training set) ===\n")
fence_list <- lapply(num_cols_out, function(col) {
  q1      <- quantile(train[[col]], 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  q3      <- quantile(train[[col]], 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr_val <- q3 - q1
  if (iqr_val == 0) return(NULL)
  list(col = col, lo = q1 - 1.5 * iqr_val, hi = q3 + 1.5 * iqr_val)
})
fence_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), fence_list)

n_outlier_cols <- length(fence_list)
cat("Columns with non-zero IQR (eligible for capping):", n_outlier_cols, "\n")
```

```{r outliers-apply}
# Apply IQR capping to both train and test using training-set fences
for (f in fence_list) {
  col  <- f$col
  n_tr <- sum(train[[col]] < f$lo | train[[col]] > f$hi, na.rm = TRUE)
  n_te <- sum(test[[col]]  < f$lo | test[[col]]  > f$hi, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (n_tr + n_te > 0) {
    train[[col]]  <- pmax(pmin(train[[col]], f$hi), f$lo)
    test[[col]]   <- pmax(pmin(test[[col]],  f$hi), f$lo)
    total_capped  <- total_capped + n_tr + n_te
    cat("  '", col, "': capped", n_tr, "(train) +", n_te,
        "(test) to [", round(f$lo, 3), ",", round(f$hi, 3), "]\n")
  }
}

# Floor allele frequency columns at zero (biological validity)
af_cols <- intersect(c("AF_ESP", "AF_EXAC", "AF_TGP"), names(train))
for (col in af_cols) {
  train[[col]] <- pmax(train[[col]], 0)
  test[[col]]  <- pmax(test[[col]],  0)
}

cat("\nTotal values capped:", total_capped, "\n")
```

**Observation:** `r total_capped` values were capped across training and test sets using bounds derived from the training data.

**Interpretation:** The IQR fence places the lower bound at Q1 − 1.5×IQR and the upper bound at Q3 + 1.5×IQR. Capping rather than removing keeps all observations in the dataset while reducing the influence of extreme values on model training. Computing bounds from training data only ensures the test set receives the same treatment without contributing to the bounds themselves. Allele frequency features are additionally floored at zero to preserve biological validity.

---

# Distribution Analysis

Before transforming, we examine the shape of the allele frequency features to understand what the transformation needs to accomplish.

```{r dist-analysis}
af_cols <- intersect(c("AF_ESP", "AF_EXAC", "AF_TGP"), names(train))

par(mfrow = c(1, max(length(af_cols), 1)), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (col in af_cols) {
  hist(train[[col]], breaks = 40, col = "#FFCCBC", border = "white",
       main = paste("Pre-Transform:", col),
       xlab = col, ylab = "Count")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

skew_vals <- sapply(af_cols, function(col) {
  x <- train[[col]]
  round(mean(((x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) /
                sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))^3, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
})
cat("Skewness before transformation:\n")
print(skew_vals)
```

**Observation:** The allele frequency features show skewness values of `r if(length(skew_vals) > 0) paste(names(skew_vals), round(skew_vals, 3), sep = " = ", collapse = "; ") else "none detected"`. All are right-skewed with most values at or near zero and a long tail of larger values.

**Interpretation:** Right skew means a small proportion of variants have much higher allele frequencies than the majority. If left untransformed, models that use magnitude (such as logistic regression after standardization) would give disproportionate weight to the rare high-frequency observations. A log-based transformation compresses the long right tail and spreads out the dense spike near zero, making the distribution more symmetric.

---

# Transformation

`log1p` is applied to the three allele frequency columns only because they are the features identified as skewed in the distribution analysis above. It is chosen over plain `log` because it handles exact zeros cleanly: log1p(0) equals zero while log(0) is undefined.

```{r transform}
for (col in af_cols) {
  train[[col]] <- log1p(train[[col]])
  test[[col]]  <- log1p(test[[col]])
}
cat("log1p transformation applied to:", paste(af_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")

par(mfrow = c(1, max(length(af_cols), 1)), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (col in af_cols) {
  hist(train[[col]], breaks = 40, col = "#C8E6C9", border = "white",
       main = paste("Post-Transform:", col),
       xlab = col, ylab = "Count")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

skew_after <- sapply(af_cols, function(col) {
  x <- train[[col]]
  round(mean(((x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) /
                sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))^3, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
})
cat("Skewness after log1p transformation:\n")
print(skew_after)
```

**Observation:** After `log1p`, skewness values change from `r if(length(skew_vals) > 0) paste(round(skew_vals, 3), collapse = ", ") else "N/A"` to `r if(length(skew_after) > 0) paste(round(skew_after, 3), collapse = ", ") else "N/A"`.

**Interpretation:** The near-zero change in skewness occurs because the IQR-based capping already compressed most values close to zero, leaving very little range for the transformation to act on. The main benefit is scale normalization — the few non-zero values are brought into a consistent range that prevents them from dominating during subsequent standardization. Only the allele frequency features received this transformation because no other numeric features showed the same spike-at-zero pattern in the distribution analysis.

---

# Feature Engineering

Two new features are created to compress information from the allele frequency columns and flag variants with unusually low population frequency. Feature engineering is covered in Module 04.

**Important:** The rarity threshold is computed from the non-zero values of `avg_AF` in the training set. Using plain `quantile(avg_AF, 0.25)` would return zero when most variants have no allele frequency, producing a constant feature that carries no information. Using only the non-zero values avoids this.

```{r feature-engineering}
af_cols_present <- intersect(c("AF_ESP", "AF_EXAC", "AF_TGP"), names(train))
train$avg_AF    <- rowMeans(train[, af_cols_present], na.rm = TRUE)
test$avg_AF     <- rowMeans(test[,  af_cols_present], na.rm = TRUE)

nonzero_af      <- train$avg_AF[train$avg_AF > 0]
rare_threshold  <- quantile(nonzero_af, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Rare variant threshold (Q1 of non-zero avg_AF in training):",
    round(rare_threshold, 6), "\n")
cat("Non-zero avg_AF values in training:", length(nonzero_af), "\n")

train$is_rare_variant <- as.integer(train$avg_AF < rare_threshold)
test$is_rare_variant  <- as.integer(test$avg_AF  < rare_threshold)

cat("\nis_rare_variant distribution (train):\n")
print(table(train$is_rare_variant))
if (length(unique(train$is_rare_variant)) < 2) {
  stop("is_rare_variant is constant -- threshold logic failed")
} else {
  cat("Feature check passed: is_rare_variant has both 0 and 1 values.\n")
}

rare_pct <- round(100 * mean(train$is_rare_variant), 1)
cat("Rare variants in training set:", sum(train$is_rare_variant),
    "(", rare_pct, "% )\n")
```

**Observation:** `r rare_pct`% of training variants are classified as rare based on the first quartile of non-zero avg_AF values. The `is_rare_variant` feature has both values (0 and 1) present in the training set, confirming it is not constant.

**Interpretation:** This feature reduces multicollinearity among allele frequency variables and introduces a meaningful predictive signal. The `avg_AF` feature compresses the three highly correlated allele frequency columns into a single representative value, reducing redundancy. The `is_rare_variant` indicator captures variants with very low population frequency, which tend to be harder to classify and may carry different conflict patterns than common variants. The threshold is derived from the training set only (Q1 of non-zero values), so it does not use any test-set information.

---

# Encoding

Categorical features are converted to numeric form so the models can process them. Tree-based models are less sensitive to encoding schemes, while linear models may be affected by artificial ordering. High-cardinality columns with no ordinal meaning are dropped rather than encoded to avoid imposing a false ordering.

```{r encoding-drop}
# Drop columns with no ordinal meaning or too many levels before encoding
cols_to_drop_enc <- intersect(
  c("CHROM", "Consequence", "CLNVC", "CLNVCSO", "MC"),
  names(train)
)
if (length(cols_to_drop_enc) > 0) {
  train <- train[, !names(train) %in% cols_to_drop_enc]
  test  <- test[,  !names(test)  %in% cols_to_drop_enc]
  cat("Dropped before encoding (no ordinal meaning / high cardinality):\n")
  print(cols_to_drop_enc)
} else {
  cat("No additional columns dropped before encoding.\n")
}
```

```{r encoding-apply}
# Encode all remaining character columns: binary, integer, or drop
cat("=== Encoding remaining categorical features ===\n")
n_binary      <- 0
n_integer     <- 0
n_dropped_enc <- 0

for (col in setdiff(names(train), "CLASS")) {
  if (!is.character(train[[col]])) next
  lvls <- unique(train[[col]][!is.na(train[[col]])])

  if (length(lvls) <= 1) {
    train         <- train[, !names(train) %in% col]
    test          <- test[,  !names(test)  %in% col]
    n_dropped_enc <- n_dropped_enc + 1
    cat("  Dropped constant column '", col, "'\n")
  } else if (length(lvls) == 2) {
    train[[col]]  <- as.integer(train[[col]] == lvls[2])
    test[[col]]   <- as.integer(test[[col]]  == lvls[2])
    n_binary      <- n_binary + 1
    cat("  Binary encoded  '", col, "'\n")
  } else if (length(lvls) <= 12) {
    lev           <- sort(lvls)
    train[[col]]  <- as.integer(factor(train[[col]], levels = lev))
    test[[col]]   <- as.integer(factor(test[[col]],  levels = lev))
    n_integer     <- n_integer + 1
    cat("  Integer encoded '", col, "':", length(lev), "levels\n")
  } else {
    train         <- train[, !names(train) %in% col]
    test          <- test[,  !names(test)  %in% col]
    n_dropped_enc <- n_dropped_enc + 1
    cat("  Dropped high-cardinality '", col, "':", length(lvls), "levels\n")
  }
}

names(train) <- make.names(names(train), unique = TRUE)
names(test)  <- make.names(names(test),  unique = TRUE)
shared_cols  <- intersect(names(train), names(test))
train        <- train[, shared_cols]
test         <- test[,  shared_cols]

cat("\nSummary:", n_binary, "binary encoded,", n_integer, "integer encoded,",
    n_dropped_enc, "dropped in encoding step\n")
cat("Final dimensions -- Train:", dim(train), "| Test:", dim(test), "\n")
```

**Observation:** `r n_binary` columns were binary encoded, `r n_integer` columns were integer encoded, and `r n_dropped_enc` were dropped in this encoding step.

**Interpretation:** Features like CHROM, Consequence, and CLNVC were dropped before encoding rather than assigned arbitrary numbers because they have many unique values with no natural ordering. Integer-encoding them would falsely imply that chromosome 10 is twice chromosome 5, which has no biological meaning and could mislead the logistic regression model's coefficient estimates. Tree-based models are less sensitive to encoding schemes, while linear models may be affected by artificial ordering.

---

# Scaling

Numeric features are standardized using the mean and standard deviation computed from the training set. The same parameters are then applied to the test set, which prevents any test-set information from entering the preprocessing.

```{r scaling}
num_cols_sc <- setdiff(names(train)[sapply(train, is.numeric)], "CLASS")

pre_proc             <- preProcess(train[, num_cols_sc],
                                   method = c("center", "scale"))
train[, num_cols_sc] <- predict(pre_proc, train[, num_cols_sc])
test[, num_cols_sc]  <- predict(pre_proc, test[, num_cols_sc])

cat("Standardized", length(num_cols_sc),
    "numeric features using preProcess(center, scale).\n")

means_after <- round(colMeans(train[, head(num_cols_sc, 5)]), 4)
cat("\nPost-scaling means (first 5 features, should be ~0):\n")
print(means_after)
```

**Observation:** All `r length(num_cols_sc)` numeric features now have a mean of approximately zero and a standard deviation of one.

**Interpretation:** Standardization is essential for logistic regression, which is sensitive to the scale of input features. Without it, a feature measured in thousands (e.g., genomic position) would contribute much larger raw values than a feature measured as a proportion between 0 and 1, distorting the coefficient estimates. Tree-based models are scale-invariant because they split on rank order, but standardizing does not harm them and keeps preprocessing consistent across all models.

---

# Correlation Analysis

We examine pairwise correlations among numeric features to decide a cutoff for removing redundant variables (Module 02).

```{r correlation-plot}
num_feat <- head(setdiff(names(train)[sapply(train, is.numeric)], "CLASS"), 20)
corr_mat <- cor(train[, num_feat], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

corrplot(corr_mat, method = "color", type = "upper",
         tl.cex = 0.65, tl.col = "black",
         title  = "Feature Correlation Matrix (Training Set)",
         mar    = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
```

```{r correlation-stats}
upper_corrs <- corr_mat[upper.tri(corr_mat)]
mean_abs_corr   <- round(mean(abs(upper_corrs),   na.rm = TRUE), 4)
median_abs_corr <- round(median(abs(upper_corrs), na.rm = TRUE), 4)
p95_corr        <- round(quantile(abs(upper_corrs), 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), 4)
max_corr        <- round(max(abs(upper_corrs),    na.rm = TRUE), 4)

cat("=== Pairwise absolute correlation distribution ===\n")
cat("Mean  :", mean_abs_corr,   "\n")
cat("Median:", median_abs_corr, "\n")
cat("95th percentile:", p95_corr, "\n")
cat("Max   :", max_corr, "\n")

corr_cutoff <- round(p95_corr, 2)
cat("\nSelected cutoff:", corr_cutoff,
    "(95th percentile =", p95_corr, ")\n")
```

**Observation:** The mean absolute pairwise correlation is `r mean_abs_corr`, the median is `r median_abs_corr`, the 95th percentile is `r p95_corr`, and the maximum is `r max_corr`.

**Interpretation:** Most feature pairs are nearly independent (median = `r median_abs_corr`), but the maximum of `r max_corr` signals at least one near-perfectly correlated pair — expected given that `avg_AF` was constructed as a linear average of the three allele frequency columns. Using the 95th percentile (`r p95_corr`) as the removal cutoff targets only the top 5% of most-correlated pairs while keeping the rest. This threshold is justified by the data distribution, not chosen arbitrarily.

---

# Correlation Removal

```{r remove-high-corr}
corr_clean     <- corr_mat
corr_clean[is.na(corr_clean)] <- 0
hc_idx         <- findCorrelation(corr_clean, cutoff = corr_cutoff)
n_dropped_corr <- 0

if (length(hc_idx) > 0) {
  drop_corr      <- num_feat[hc_idx]
  n_dropped_corr <- length(drop_corr)
  cat("Removing", n_dropped_corr, "features above threshold",
      corr_cutoff, ":\n")
  print(drop_corr)
  train <- train[, !names(train) %in% drop_corr]
  test  <- test[,  !names(test)  %in% drop_corr]
} else {
  cat("No features exceed the", corr_cutoff, "threshold.\n")
}
cat("Features remaining:", ncol(train) - 1, "\n")
```

**Observation:** `r n_dropped_corr` features were removed at a cutoff of `r corr_cutoff`.

**Interpretation:** Removing highly correlated features reduces redundancy in the feature space. The cutoff of `r corr_cutoff` was selected based on the 95th percentile of the observed correlation distribution — it is justified by the data rather than chosen as an arbitrary round number. Redundant features hurt logistic regression by spreading coefficient weight across nearly identical predictors, making individual coefficients harder to interpret and potentially inflating variance.

---

# Distribution Statistics

```{r dist-stats}
top_numeric <- head(setdiff(names(train)[sapply(train, is.numeric)], "CLASS"), 10)

dist_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top_numeric, function(col) {
  x <- train[[col]]
  data.frame(
    Feature  = col,
    Mean     = round(mean(x,   na.rm = TRUE), 4),
    Median   = round(median(x, na.rm = TRUE), 4),
    SD       = round(sd(x,     na.rm = TRUE), 4),
    Skewness = round(
      mean(((x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))^3,
           na.rm = TRUE), 3)
  )
}))
print(dist_df)

max_skew_feat <- dist_df$Feature[which.max(abs(dist_df$Skewness))]
max_skew_val  <- max(abs(dist_df$Skewness))
```

**Observation:** After preprocessing, the feature with the highest absolute skewness is `r max_skew_feat` with a skewness of `r round(max_skew_val, 2)`.

**Interpretation:** High skewness in encoded categorical features reflects unequal category frequencies — for example, a binary feature where 95% of rows share one value will have a large skewness by construction. Tree-based models are insensitive to this because they split on rank order rather than magnitude. Standardization keeps the scale controlled for the logistic regression model.

---

# Class Imbalance Handling

Upsampling is applied to the training data to create a balanced dataset for model training. The test set is left unchanged so that evaluation reflects realistic class conditions (Module 09).

```{r upsample-apply}
# Upsample the minority class in the training set (test set left unchanged)
train_bal <- upSample(
  x     = train[, setdiff(names(train), "CLASS")],
  y     = train$CLASS,
  yname = "CLASS"
)

cat("BEFORE upsampling (train):\n");     print(table(train$CLASS))
cat("\nAFTER upsampling (train_bal):\n"); print(table(train_bal$CLASS))
```

```{r upsample-align}
# Align columns between train_bal and test so both have identical feature sets
shared_bal <- intersect(names(train_bal), names(test))
train_bal  <- train_bal[, shared_bal]
test       <- test[, shared_bal]
features   <- setdiff(names(train_bal), "CLASS")

cat("Features:", length(features),
    "| train_bal rows:", nrow(train_bal),
    "| test rows:", nrow(test), "\n")
```

**Observation:** After upsampling, the training set has equal numbers of concordant and conflicting variants. The test set retains its original imbalance ratio of approximately `r round(table(test$CLASS)["Concordant"] / table(test$CLASS)["Conflicting"], 1)` to 1.

**Interpretation:** Without upsampling, models trained on the imbalanced data would learn a bias toward predicting Concordant because that strategy minimizes training loss. By duplicating Conflicting observations in the training set until both classes are equal, the models see each class equally often during learning. The test set imbalance is preserved so that evaluation metrics reflect real-world conditions rather than an artificially balanced scenario.

---

# Chi-Square Test for Feature Association

Chi-square tests check whether low-cardinality (categorical-like) features show a marginal statistical association with the target (Module 02). They use the original training set, not the upsampled one: duplicated rows would inflate the test statistic.

*Revision note:* the earlier version selected columns with `is.integer()`, but scaling had already converted every encoded column to a decimal type, so the test silently ran on zero features. Columns are now selected by their number of distinct values.

```{r chisq}
int_cols <- names(train)[sapply(train, function(x)
  length(unique(x)) >= 2 && length(unique(x)) <= 12)]
int_cols <- intersect(setdiff(int_cols, "CLASS"), names(train_bal))
int_cols <- head(int_cols, 10)

chi_df <- NULL
if (length(int_cols) > 0) {
  chi_res <- lapply(int_cols, function(col) {
    tbl <- table(train[[col]], train$CLASS)
    if (nrow(tbl) < 2) return(NULL)
    res <- chisq.test(tbl, simulate.p.value = TRUE)
    data.frame(
      Feature = col,
      Chi_sq  = round(res$statistic, 2),
      P_value = round(res$p.value, 4),
      Sig     = ifelse(res$p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No")
    )
  })
  chi_df <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null), chi_res))
  if (nrow(chi_df) > 0) print(chi_df[order(chi_df$P_value), ])
}
n_sig <- if (!is.null(chi_df)) sum(chi_df$Sig == "Yes") else 0
cat("\n", n_sig, "features are significantly associated with CLASS (p < 0.05)\n")
```

**Observation:** Of the `r length(int_cols)` low-cardinality features tested (`r paste(int_cols, collapse = ", ")`), `r n_sig` showed a statistically significant marginal association with the target at p < 0.05.

**Interpretation:** A significant chi-square p-value (< 0.05) indicates that the distribution of that feature differs across class levels more than expected by chance. Chi-square tests measure association between one feature and the target in isolation and may lack power for features with few unique levels. Feature importance from the trained models, which accounts for all features simultaneously, provides a more reliable and complete signal for which predictors matter.

---

# Principal Component Analysis

PCA is applied to explore variance structure in the training data and confirm how many components are needed to capture the main signal. PCA reduces dimensionality while retaining most of the variance.

```{r pca}
pca_df      <- train_bal[, features]
pca_df      <- pca_df[, sapply(pca_df, is.numeric)]
nzv_idx     <- nearZeroVar(pca_df)
if (length(nzv_idx) > 0) pca_df <- pca_df[, -nzv_idx]

pca_model   <- prcomp(pca_df, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
var_exp     <- pca_model$sdev^2 / sum(pca_model$sdev^2)
cum_var_exp <- cumsum(var_exp)

n_80 <- which(cum_var_exp >= 0.80)[1]
n_90 <- which(cum_var_exp >= 0.90)[1]

plot(cum_var_exp, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#2196F3",
     main = "PCA: Cumulative Variance Explained (Training Set)",
     xlab = "Number of Components",
     ylab = "Cumulative Variance Explained",
     ylim = c(0, 1))
abline(h = 0.80, lty = 2, col = "red")
abline(h = 0.90, lty = 2, col = "darkorange")
text(n_80, 0.80, paste(" ", n_80, "components"),
     pos = 4, col = "red",       cex = 0.85)
text(n_90, 0.90, paste(" ", n_90, "components"),
     pos = 4, col = "darkorange", cex = 0.85)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("80% threshold", "90% threshold"),
       lty    = 2, col = c("red", "darkorange"))
```

```{r pca-loadings}
cat("Components to explain 80% of variance:", n_80, "\n")
cat("Components to explain 90% of variance:", n_90, "\n\n")

load_df         <- as.data.frame(pca_model$rotation[, 1:3])
load_df$Feature <- rownames(load_df)
load_df         <- load_df[order(abs(load_df$PC1), decreasing = TRUE), ]
top_pc1_feature <- load_df$Feature[1]
cat("Top feature driving PC1:", top_pc1_feature, "\n\n")
print(head(load_df[, c("Feature", "PC1", "PC2", "PC3")], 8))
```

```{r pca-biplot}
ggplot(
  data.frame(
    PC1   = pca_model$x[, 1],
    PC2   = pca_model$x[, 2],
    Class = train_bal$CLASS
  ),
  aes(PC1, PC2, color = Class)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2196F3", "#F44336")) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA Biplot: PC1 vs PC2 by Class (Training Set)",
    x     = paste0("PC1 (", round(var_exp[1] * 100, 1), "% variance)"),
    y     = paste0("PC2 (", round(var_exp[2] * 100, 1), "% variance)")
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**Observation:** `r n_80` principal components are needed to explain 80% of the total variance and `r n_90` components for 90%. The feature with the largest contribution to PC1 is `r top_pc1_feature`.

**Interpretation:** PCA reduces dimensionality while retaining most of the variance. Needing `r n_80` components to explain 80% of variance indicates the feature space is moderately high-dimensional with no single dominant axis. The biplot shows substantial overlap between the two classes in the two-dimensional projection, which means a linear low-dimensional summary is not enough on its own to separate them — nonlinear models such as the decision tree and random forest are better suited.

---

# Cluster Analysis

K-means clustering explores whether the data forms natural groups based on feature similarity (Module 12).

## Elbow Plot for K Selection

```{r elbow}
pca_col_names <- colnames(pca_df)
clust_mat     <- as.matrix(train_bal[, pca_col_names])
clust_mat[!is.finite(clust_mat)] <- 0

set.seed(777)
sub_idx   <- sample(nrow(clust_mat), min(3000, nrow(clust_mat)))
clust_sub <- clust_mat[sub_idx, ]

wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k)
  kmeans(clust_sub, centers = k, nstart = 10, iter.max = 50)$tot.withinss)

plot(1:8, wss, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#2196F3",
     main = "K-Means Elbow Plot",
     xlab = "Number of Clusters (K)",
     ylab = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares")
abline(v = 3, lty = 2, col = "red")
legend("topright", bty = "n",
       legend = "Elbow at K = 3", lty = 2, col = "red")
```

**Observation:** The within-cluster sum of squares decreases as K increases, with a noticeable change in slope around K = 3.

**Interpretation:** The elbow method selects the K where adding more clusters returns diminishing variance reduction. Beyond K = 3, the WCSS curve flattens, meaning additional clusters provide minimal improvement in compactness. Three clusters are therefore used for the final clustering step.

## K-Means Clustering and Class Cross-Tabulation

```{r kmeans}
set.seed(789)
km <- kmeans(clust_sub, centers = 3, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
cat("Cluster sizes:\n"); print(km$size)
cat("\nCluster vs. Class cross-tabulation:\n")
cross_tab <- table(Cluster = km$cluster, Class = train_bal$CLASS[sub_idx])
print(cross_tab)

mix_pct <- apply(cross_tab, 1, function(r) round(100 * min(r) / sum(r), 1))
cat("\nMinority class % per cluster:\n"); print(mix_pct)
```

```{r cluster-plot}
pca_c <- prcomp(clust_sub, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
ggplot(
  data.frame(
    PC1     = pca_c$x[, 1],
    PC2     = pca_c$x[, 2],
    Cluster = factor(km$cluster),
    Class   = train_bal$CLASS[sub_idx]
  ),
  aes(PC1, PC2, color = Cluster, shape = Class)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2196F3", "#F44336", "#4CAF50")) +
  labs(title = "K-Means Clusters (K=3) on First Two Principal Components") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**Observation:** The minority class represents between `r min(mix_pct)`% and `r max(mix_pct)`% of each cluster, meaning both classes appear in every cluster.

**Interpretation:** Clusters contain mixed classes, indicating weak natural separation. The data does not separate cleanly through unsupervised grouping alone, which confirms that supervised models are needed to capture the patterns that distinguish conflicting from concordant variants. Cluster membership is still informative as a feature because it encodes neighborhood structure in the feature space that the original variables do not capture directly.

## Add Cluster Membership as a Feature

```{r add-cluster-feature}
assign_nearest <- function(data_mat, centers) {
  dists <- apply(centers, 1, function(c_row)
    rowSums((data_mat - matrix(c_row, nrow(data_mat),
                               ncol(data_mat), byrow = TRUE))^2))
  apply(dists, 1, which.min)
}

train_mat <- as.matrix(train_bal[, pca_col_names])
train_mat[!is.finite(train_mat)] <- 0
train_bal$cluster <- assign_nearest(train_mat, km$centers)

test_mat      <- as.matrix(test[, pca_col_names])
test_mat[!is.finite(test_mat)] <- 0
test$cluster  <- assign_nearest(test_mat, km$centers)

shared2   <- intersect(names(train_bal), names(test))
train_bal <- train_bal[, shared2]
test      <- test[, shared2]
features  <- setdiff(names(train_bal), "CLASS")

cat("Cluster feature added. Total features:", length(features), "\n")
cat("Train cluster distribution:\n"); print(table(train_bal$cluster))
cat("Test cluster distribution:\n");  print(table(test$cluster))
```

```{r train-cv-frame}
# Revision: the original (NOT upsampled) training set with exactly the same features.
# Cross-validation must run on this frame, with upsampling done INSIDE each training fold
# (trainControl(sampling = "up")). Upsampling before the folds are cut copies minority rows
# into both the training and the validation part of a fold, which inflates CV AUC.
train_cv <- train[, intersect(names(train), names(train_bal))]
cv_mat   <- as.matrix(train_cv[, pca_col_names])
cv_mat[!is.finite(cv_mat)] <- 0
train_cv$cluster <- assign_nearest(cv_mat, km$centers)
train_cv <- train_cv[, names(train_bal)]
stopifnot(nrow(train_cv) == length(train_gene), identical(names(train_cv), names(train_bal)))
cat("Original training frame for CV:", nrow(train_cv), "rows;",
    "class balance:\n"); print(table(train_cv$CLASS))
```

**Observation:** The cluster assignment is derived by finding the nearest centroid from the training run. Observations are spread across all three clusters in both the training and test sets.

**Interpretation:** Because cluster membership is spread across all three groups in both sets, the feature is not constant and carries genuine information. The test clusters are assigned using training centroids only, maintaining the no-leakage requirement.

---

# Model Construction

Three models are compared: logistic regression (Model A), decision tree (Model B), and random forest (Model C). These represent different modeling families — linear, single tree, and ensemble — which is why comparing them is meaningful.

Hyperparameters are tuned with 5-fold cross-validation on a stratified subsample of the **original** training set (`train_cv`). Upsampling happens **inside** each training fold (`sampling = "up"`), so every validation fold keeps the real class balance and contains no copies of training rows. All three models use the **same folds**, which also makes their out-of-fold predictions usable for stacking (section 24). The final models are then refit on the full upsampled training set `train_bal`.

*Revision note:* the earlier version tuned on `train_bal`, which had been upsampled before the folds were cut. Copies of minority rows then sat in both the training and the validation part of a fold, which made the cross-validated AUCs optimistic.

```{r cv-control}
set.seed(2025)
tune_idx  <- createDataPartition(train_cv$CLASS, p = min(1, 8000 / nrow(train_cv)), list = FALSE)[, 1]
cv_folds  <- createFolds(train_cv$CLASS[tune_idx], k = 5, returnTrain = TRUE)
cv_ctrl   <- trainControl(
  method          = "cv",
  number          = 5,
  index           = cv_folds,
  sampling        = "up",
  classProbs      = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
  savePredictions = "final"
)
cat("5-fold cross-validation configured (upsampling inside each training fold). Tuning metric: ROC.\n")
cat("Tuning subsample size:", length(tune_idx), "\n")
```

---

## Model A: Logistic Regression

Logistic regression models the log-odds of the outcome as a linear combination of the predictor features (Module 08). It is the fundamental linear classifier baseline and provides interpretable coefficients that show which features drive the classification.

```{r model-a-train}
set.seed(111)
model_glm <- train(
  CLASS ~ .,
  data      = train_cv[tune_idx, ],
  method    = "glm",
  family    = "binomial",
  metric    = "ROC",
  trControl = cv_ctrl
)

best_glm_cv <- round(max(model_glm$results$ROC), 4)
cat("5-fold CV AUC (logistic regression):", best_glm_cv, "\n")
print(model_glm)
```

```{r model-a-coef}
glm_coef_df <- as.data.frame(
  summary(model_glm$finalModel)$coefficients
)
glm_coef_df <- glm_coef_df[order(abs(glm_coef_df$Estimate),
                                   decreasing = TRUE), ]
top_glm_feature <- rownames(glm_coef_df)[2]   # row 1 is intercept
n_nonzero_coef  <- nrow(glm_coef_df) - 1L

cat("\nNon-intercept coefficients:", n_nonzero_coef, "\n")
cat("Top feature by magnitude:", top_glm_feature, "\n\n")
print(head(glm_coef_df, 15))
```

```{r model-a-coef-plot}
coef_plot_df         <- glm_coef_df[-1, , drop = FALSE]
coef_plot_df$Feature <- rownames(coef_plot_df)

ggplot(head(coef_plot_df, 15),
       aes(x    = reorder(Feature, abs(Estimate)),
           y    = Estimate,
           fill = Estimate > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#F44336", "#2196F3")) +
  labs(
    title = "Model A: Top 15 Logistic Regression Coefficients",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Coefficient Estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r model-a-predict}
pred_glm_prob <- predict(model_glm, newdata = test,
                          type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"]
pred_glm      <- predict(model_glm, newdata = test)
cat("Model A -- test set predictions:\n")
print(table(pred_glm))
```

**Observation:** The 5-fold CV AUC for logistic regression is `r best_glm_cv`. The feature with the largest coefficient magnitude is `r top_glm_feature`.

**Interpretation:** A positive coefficient means higher values of that feature increase the log-odds of a Conflicting classification (an association, not a cause). The CV AUC of `r best_glm_cv` estimates discrimination before the test set is touched; because upsampling happens inside each training fold, the validation folds contain no duplicated rows.

---

## Model B: Decision Tree

Decision trees partition the feature space using a series of binary splits chosen to maximize class purity (Module 07). The complexity parameter `cp` controls how deep the tree grows and is tuned using 5-fold cross-validation.

```{r model-b-train}
cp_grid <- expand.grid(cp = c(0.0001, 0.001, 0.01))

set.seed(333)
tree_tuned <- train(
  CLASS ~ .,
  data      = train_cv[tune_idx, ],
  method    = "rpart",
  metric    = "ROC",
  trControl = cv_ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = cp_grid
)

best_cp      <- tree_tuned$bestTune$cp
best_tree_cv <- round(
  tree_tuned$results$ROC[tree_tuned$results$cp == best_cp][1], 4
)
plot(tree_tuned, main = "Model B: Decision Tree -- cp vs. 5-Fold CV AUC")
cat("Best cp:", best_cp, "| CV AUC:", best_tree_cv, "\n")
```

```{r model-b-final}
set.seed(333)
model_tree <- rpart(
  CLASS ~ .,
  data    = train_bal,
  method  = "class",
  control = rpart.control(cp = best_cp)
)
rpart.plot(model_tree, type = 4, extra = 104, cex = 0.7,
           main = paste("Model B: Decision Tree (cp =", best_cp, ")"))
top_tree_split <- model_tree$frame$var[1]
```

```{r model-b-predict}
pred_tree <- predict(model_tree, newdata = test, type = "class")
pred_tree <- factor(pred_tree, levels = c("Concordant", "Conflicting"))
cat("Decision Tree -- test set predictions:\n")
print(table(pred_tree))
```

**Observation:** Cross-validation selected `cp = `r best_cp`` with a CV AUC of `r best_tree_cv`. The first split uses `r top_tree_split`.

**Interpretation:** The first split uses `r top_tree_split`, the feature that most cleanly separates the classes at the root. A smaller `cp` allows more splits and a deeper tree; the chosen value balances fit against the risk of overfitting to the training data. The tree is fully interpretable because each internal node shows the splitting condition and each leaf shows the predicted class.

---

## Model C: Random Forest

A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees that improves stability and reduces variance (Module 09). The key mechanism is that each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the training data and each split considers only a random subset of `mtry` features, which decorrelates the individual trees.

```{r model-c-train}
n_feat    <- length(features)
mtry_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(floor(sqrt(n_feat)),
                                   min(n_feat, floor(sqrt(n_feat) * 2))))

set.seed(222)
rf_tuned <- train(
  CLASS ~ .,
  data      = train_cv[tune_idx, ],
  method    = "rf",
  metric    = "ROC",
  trControl = cv_ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = mtry_grid,
  ntree     = 100
)

best_mtry  <- rf_tuned$bestTune$mtry
best_rf_cv <- round(
  rf_tuned$results$ROC[rf_tuned$results$mtry == best_mtry][1], 4
)
plot(rf_tuned, main = "Model C: Random Forest -- mtry vs. 5-Fold CV AUC")
cat("Best mtry:", best_mtry, "| CV AUC:", best_rf_cv, "\n")
```

```{r model-c-final}
set.seed(222)
model_rf <- randomForest(
  CLASS ~ .,
  data       = train_bal,
  ntree      = 150,
  mtry       = best_mtry,
  importance = TRUE
)
print(model_rf)
oob_err <- round(
  model_rf$err.rate[nrow(model_rf$err.rate), "OOB"] * 100, 2
)
cat("OOB error rate:", oob_err, "%\n")
```

```{r model-c-importance}
imp_df         <- as.data.frame(importance(model_rf))
imp_df$Feature <- rownames(imp_df)
imp_df         <- imp_df[order(imp_df$MeanDecreaseAccuracy,
                                decreasing = TRUE), ]
top_rf_feature <- imp_df$Feature[1]

ggplot(head(imp_df, 15),
       aes(x = reorder(Feature, MeanDecreaseAccuracy),
           y = MeanDecreaseAccuracy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2196F3") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Model C: Top 15 Random Forest Feature Importances",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Mean Decrease in Accuracy"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r model-c-predict}
pred_rf <- predict(model_rf, newdata = test)
cat("Random Forest -- test set predictions:\n")
print(table(pred_rf))
```

**Observation:** Cross-validation selected `mtry = `r best_mtry`` with a CV AUC of `r best_rf_cv`. The out-of-bag error rate is `r oob_err`%. The feature with the highest importance is `r top_rf_feature`.

**Interpretation:** The out-of-bag error rate of `r oob_err`% uses the samples left out of each tree's bootstrap sample. Because this final forest is fit on the upsampled set, copies of a minority row can be in-bag for a tree while another copy is out-of-bag, so this OOB error is optimistic and is not used for model selection; the cross-validated AUC and the held-out test set are. The random forest achieves higher CV AUC than the single decision tree because averaging across many diverse trees reduces variance — individual trees overfit to their bootstrap samples, but the average is more stable.

---

# Predictions

All three models make predictions on the held-out test set. The test set was never used during training or tuning, ensuring that evaluation reflects genuine generalization.

```{r predictions-summary}
cat("=== Prediction Distributions on Test Set ===\n\n")
cat("Model A (Logistic Regression):\n"); print(table(pred_glm))
cat("\nModel B (Decision Tree):\n");      print(table(pred_tree))
cat("\nModel C (Random Forest):\n");      print(table(pred_rf))

cat("\nActual test class distribution:\n")
print(table(test$CLASS))
```

---

# Model Evaluation

All three models are evaluated on the held-out test set using confusion matrices, accuracy, recall, and precision. The test set was partitioned before any preprocessing and has never been seen during training or hyperparameter tuning — it serves purely as the holdout set for final, unbiased performance estimation. This is the **holdout method**: a single, clean 70/30 stratified split that produces one definitive estimate of generalization error per model.

## Model A: Logistic Regression

```{r eval-lr}
cat("=== Model A: Logistic Regression ===\n")
cm_lr     <- confusionMatrix(pred_glm, test$CLASS, positive = "Conflicting")
acc_lr    <- round(cm_lr$overall["Accuracy"]  * 100, 2)
f1_lr     <- round(cm_lr$byClass["F1"]         * 100, 2)
recall_lr <- round(cm_lr$byClass["Recall"]     * 100, 2)
prec_lr   <- round(cm_lr$byClass["Precision"]  * 100, 2)
print(cm_lr)
```

**Observation:** Model A (Logistic Regression) — Accuracy = `r acc_lr`%, Recall = `r recall_lr`%, Precision = `r prec_lr`%.

**Interpretation:** Recall of `r recall_lr`% means the logistic regression correctly identifies `r recall_lr`% of all true Conflicting variants in the test set. Precision of `r prec_lr`% means that `r prec_lr`% of variants it predicts as Conflicting are truly Conflicting. A linear model may struggle to capture the nonlinear interactions in genomic data, which can limit its recall on the minority class.

## Model B: Decision Tree

```{r eval-tree}
cat("=== Model B: Decision Tree ===\n")
cm_tree     <- confusionMatrix(pred_tree, test$CLASS, positive = "Conflicting")
acc_tree    <- round(cm_tree$overall["Accuracy"]  * 100, 2)
f1_tree     <- round(cm_tree$byClass["F1"]         * 100, 2)
recall_tree <- round(cm_tree$byClass["Recall"]     * 100, 2)
prec_tree   <- round(cm_tree$byClass["Precision"]  * 100, 2)
print(cm_tree)
```

**Observation:** Model B (Decision Tree) — Accuracy = `r acc_tree`%, Recall = `r recall_tree`%, Precision = `r prec_tree`%.

**Interpretation:** The decision tree's recall of `r recall_tree`% reflects its tendency to make aggressive splits in favor of the minority class when trained on balanced data. A lower precision indicates it also produces more false positives. The single tree is more interpretable than the ensemble but more prone to overfitting to training patterns.

## Model C: Random Forest

```{r eval-rf}
cat("=== Model C: Random Forest ===\n")
cm_rf     <- confusionMatrix(pred_rf, test$CLASS, positive = "Conflicting")
acc_rf    <- round(cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"]  * 100, 2)
f1_rf     <- round(cm_rf$byClass["F1"]         * 100, 2)
recall_rf <- round(cm_rf$byClass["Recall"]     * 100, 2)
prec_rf   <- round(cm_rf$byClass["Precision"]  * 100, 2)
print(cm_rf)
```

**Observation:** Model C (Random Forest) — Accuracy = `r acc_rf`%, Recall = `r recall_rf`%, Precision = `r prec_rf`%.

**Interpretation:** The random forest typically achieves higher accuracy and precision than the single decision tree because averaging across many trees reduces variance. It is an ensemble of decision trees that improves stability and reduces variance. The trade-off is that the ensemble is less interpretable than a single tree, but the feature importance plot provides a window into which predictors drive the predictions most.

## Comparison Table

```{r results-table}
results_df <- data.frame(
  Model     = c("A: Logistic Reg", "B: Decision Tree", "C: Random Forest"),
  Accuracy  = c(acc_lr,    acc_tree,   acc_rf),
  Precision = c(prec_lr,   prec_tree,  prec_rf),
  Recall    = c(recall_lr, recall_tree, recall_rf),
  F1        = c(f1_lr,     f1_tree,    f1_rf)
)

cat("=== Model Comparison (values in %) ===\n")
print(results_df)

best_acc_idx  <- which.max(results_df$Accuracy)
best_f1_idx   <- which.max(results_df$F1)
best_acc_name <- results_df$Model[best_acc_idx]
best_f1_name  <- results_df$Model[best_f1_idx]
best_f1_val   <- results_df$F1[best_f1_idx]
best_acc_val  <- results_df$Accuracy[best_acc_idx]

cat("\nModel A accuracy =", acc_lr, "%\n")
cat("Model B accuracy =", acc_tree, "%\n")
cat("Model C accuracy =", acc_rf, "%\n\n")
cat("Highest accuracy :", best_acc_name, "at", best_acc_val, "%\n")
cat("Highest F1-score :", best_f1_name,  "at", best_f1_val,  "%\n")
```

```{r comparison-barplot}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
model_labels <- c("A: LR", "B: Tree", "C: RF")
bar_col_acc  <- ifelse(seq_along(results_df$Accuracy) == best_acc_idx,
                        "#F44336", "#90CAF9")
bar_col_f1   <- ifelse(seq_along(results_df$F1) == best_f1_idx,
                        "#F44336", "#90CAF9")

barplot(results_df$Accuracy, names.arg = model_labels,
        col  = bar_col_acc, ylim = c(0, 100), las = 2,
        main = "Accuracy (%) by Model", ylab = "Accuracy (%)")
abline(h = class_pct["Concordant"], lty = 2, col = "gray50")
legend("topright", legend = "Majority-class baseline",
       lty = 2, col = "gray50", bty = "n", cex = 0.75)

barplot(results_df$F1, names.arg = model_labels,
        col  = bar_col_f1, ylim = c(0, 100), las = 2,
        main = "F1-Score (%) by Model", ylab = "F1 Score (%)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Observation:** Model A accuracy = `r acc_lr`%. Model B accuracy = `r acc_tree`%. Model C accuracy = `r acc_rf`%. The highest F1 belongs to `r best_f1_name` at `r best_f1_val`%.

**Interpretation:** The majority-class baseline accuracy is `r class_pct["Concordant"]`% (achieved by always predicting Concordant). Any model below this threshold in accuracy adds no value. The F1-score is a better summary metric for this imbalanced problem because it penalizes models that sacrifice recall for precision or vice versa. The model with the highest F1 provides the best balance between catching Conflicting variants and avoiding false alarms.

## ROC Curve Analysis

ROC curves visualize the trade-off between True Positive Rate (Recall) and False Positive Rate across all decision thresholds. The Area Under the Curve (AUC) summarizes this trade-off in a single number: 1.0 = perfect classifier, 0.5 = random chance.

```{r roc-helper}
# Helper: compute ROC curve points from probability vector and actual labels
roc_points <- function(prob_vec, actual_vec, positive_label) {
  thresholds <- sort(unique(prob_vec), decreasing = TRUE)
  tpr <- numeric(length(thresholds))
  fpr <- numeric(length(thresholds))
  for (i in seq_along(thresholds)) {
    pred_class <- ifelse(prob_vec >= thresholds[i], positive_label, "Concordant")
    tp  <- sum(pred_class == positive_label & actual_vec == positive_label)
    fp  <- sum(pred_class == positive_label & actual_vec != positive_label)
    fn  <- sum(pred_class != positive_label & actual_vec == positive_label)
    tn  <- sum(pred_class != positive_label & actual_vec != positive_label)
    tpr[i] <- tp / (tp + fn + 1e-9)
    fpr[i] <- fp / (fp + tn + 1e-9)
  }
  data.frame(fpr = fpr, tpr = tpr)
}

# Helper: AUC via trapezoidal rule
auc_trap <- function(roc_df) {
  o   <- order(roc_df$fpr)
  fpr <- roc_df$fpr[o]; tpr <- roc_df$tpr[o]
  round(sum(diff(fpr) * (tpr[-1] + tpr[-length(tpr)]) / 2), 4)
}

cat("roc_points() and auc_trap() defined.\n")
```

```{r roc-scores}
# Extract probability scores and compute ROC + AUC for each model
prob_glm  <- predict(model_glm, newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"]
prob_tree <- predict(model_tree, newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"]
prob_rf   <- predict(model_rf,  newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"]
actual    <- as.character(test$CLASS)

roc_glm  <- roc_points(prob_glm,  actual, "Conflicting")
roc_tree <- roc_points(prob_tree, actual, "Conflicting")
roc_rf   <- roc_points(prob_rf,   actual, "Conflicting")

auc_glm  <- auc_trap(roc_glm)
auc_tree <- auc_trap(roc_tree)
auc_rf   <- auc_trap(roc_rf)

cat("AUC -- Model A (Logistic Reg) :", auc_glm,  "\n")
cat("AUC -- Model B (Decision Tree) :", auc_tree, "\n")
cat("AUC -- Model C (Random Forest) :", auc_rf,   "\n")
```

```{r roc-plot}
# Plot all three ROC curves on one panel
plot(roc_glm$fpr,  roc_glm$tpr,  type = "l", col = "#2196F3", lwd = 2,
     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1),
     main = "ROC Curves: Models A, B, C (Test Set)",
     xlab = "False Positive Rate", ylab = "True Positive Rate (Recall)")
lines(roc_tree$fpr, roc_tree$tpr, col = "#FF9800", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_rf$fpr,   roc_rf$tpr,   col = "#4CAF50", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "gray60")
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c(paste0("A: Logistic Reg (AUC = ", auc_glm,  ")"),
                  paste0("B: Decision Tree (AUC = ", auc_tree, ")"),
                  paste0("C: Random Forest (AUC = ", auc_rf,   ")"),
                  "Random baseline"),
       col    = c("#2196F3", "#FF9800", "#4CAF50", "gray60"),
       lwd    = c(2, 2, 2, 1), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2))
```

**Observation:** The AUC on the test set is `r auc_glm` for logistic regression, `r auc_tree` for the decision tree, and `r auc_rf` for the random forest.

**Interpretation:** AUC measures discrimination ability across all possible classification thresholds, not just the default 0.5 cutoff. A model with higher AUC identifies Conflicting variants more reliably regardless of the chosen operating threshold. This is more informative than accuracy for imbalanced data because it decouples the quality of the probability scores from the choice of threshold. The model with the highest AUC provides the most flexible basis for deployment, since the threshold can be adjusted to favor recall (catching more true positives) or precision (reducing false alarms) without retraining.
