# Cross-Validation Summary

```{r cv-summary}
best_tree_auc <- round(
  tree_tuned$results$ROC[tree_tuned$results$cp == best_cp][1], 4
)
best_rf_auc   <- round(
  rf_tuned$results$ROC[rf_tuned$results$mtry == best_mtry][1], 4
)

cat("=== 5-Fold Cross-Validation AUC Summary ===\n\n")
cat("Model A (Logistic Regression) -- CV AUC:", best_glm_cv,  "\n")
cat("Model B (Decision Tree)       -- CV AUC:", best_tree_auc,"\n")
cat("Model C (Random Forest)       -- CV AUC:", best_rf_auc,  "\n")

cv_model_names <- c("A: Logistic Reg", "B: Decision Tree", "C: Random Forest")
cv_aucs        <- c(best_glm_cv, best_tree_auc, best_rf_auc)
cv_best_idx    <- which.max(cv_aucs)
cv_bar_colors  <- ifelse(seq_along(cv_aucs) == cv_best_idx,
                          "#F44336", "#2196F3")

barplot(cv_aucs, names.arg = cv_model_names,
        col  = cv_bar_colors, ylim = c(0, 1), las = 2,
        main = "5-Fold CV AUC: Models A, B, C",
        ylab = "AUC")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Best CV AUC", "Others", "Random baseline (0.5)"),
       fill   = c("#F44336", "#2196F3", NA),
       lty    = c(NA, NA, 2),
       col    = c(NA, NA, "gray50"))

cv_winner <- cv_model_names[cv_best_idx]
cat("\nBest CV AUC:", cv_winner, "at", max(cv_aucs), "\n")
```

**Observation:** The 5-fold CV AUC values during tuning were: Model A = `r best_glm_cv`, Model B = `r best_tree_auc`, Model C = `r best_rf_auc`. `r cv_winner` achieved the highest CV AUC of `r max(cv_aucs)`.

**Interpretation:** Cross-validation ensures model stability and prevents overfitting. The CV AUC is computed on held-out validation folds that are not used in training, so it is an unbiased estimate of generalization before the test set is ever touched. Tuning decisions (cp for the tree, mtry for the forest) are based on CV AUC rather than training accuracy so that the selected hyperparameters generalize rather than overfit to the training set.

---

# Bagging: Homogeneous Ensemble

Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) trains multiple copies of the **same** model type on different bootstrap samples and combines their predictions by majority vote. This reduces variance without increasing bias. The `ipred::bagging()` function implements bagging over decision trees (Module 09).

Each bootstrap sample is drawn with replacement from the training data, so each bagged tree sees a slightly different dataset. Predictions are aggregated by majority vote across all trees.

The validation split is carved from the **original** training set first, and only the remaining 80% is upsampled. *Revision note:* the earlier version split the already-upsampled set, so copies of the same minority row could appear in both `bag_train` and `bag_val`, which inflated the validation score.

```{r bagging-split}
library(ipred)

# Stratified 80/20 split of the ORIGINAL training set; upsample the 80% only
set.seed(444)
bag_val_idx <- createDataPartition(train_cv$CLASS, p = 0.20, list = FALSE)[, 1]
bag_val     <- train_cv[ bag_val_idx, ]
bag_train   <- upSample(x = train_cv[-bag_val_idx, setdiff(names(train_cv), "CLASS")],
                        y = train_cv$CLASS[-bag_val_idx], yname = "CLASS")

cat("Bagging split -- bag_train:", nrow(bag_train),
    "| bag_val:", nrow(bag_val), "\n")
```

```{r bagging-train}
# Train 25-tree bagged decision tree on bag_train only
model_bag <- bagging(
  CLASS ~ .,
  data   = bag_train,    # 80% of balanced training data
  nbagg  = 25,           # 25 bootstrap replicates of a decision tree
  coob   = TRUE          # compute OOB error estimate from bootstrap samples
)

oob_bag <- round(model_bag$err * 100, 2)
cat("Bagged decision tree (nbagg = 25)\n")
cat("OOB error rate:", oob_bag, "%\n")
```

```{r bagging-evaluate}
# Validate on internal validation set, then evaluate on held-out test set
pred_bag_val <- predict(model_bag, newdata = bag_val)
pred_bag_val <- factor(pred_bag_val, levels = c("Concordant", "Conflicting"))
cm_bag_val   <- confusionMatrix(pred_bag_val, bag_val$CLASS, positive = "Conflicting")

cat("=== Bagged Tree -- Validation Set (internal, pre-test) ===\n")
cat("Validation Accuracy :", round(cm_bag_val$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("Validation Recall   :", round(cm_bag_val$byClass["Recall"]   * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("Validation Precision:", round(cm_bag_val$byClass["Precision"]* 100, 2), "%\n")

pred_bag <- predict(model_bag, newdata = test)
pred_bag <- factor(pred_bag, levels = c("Concordant", "Conflicting"))

cm_bag     <- confusionMatrix(pred_bag, test$CLASS, positive = "Conflicting")
acc_bag    <- round(cm_bag$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 2)
f1_bag     <- round(cm_bag$byClass["F1"]        * 100, 2)
recall_bag <- round(cm_bag$byClass["Recall"]    * 100, 2)
prec_bag   <- round(cm_bag$byClass["Precision"] * 100, 2)

cat("\n=== Bagged Tree -- Test Set ===\n")
print(cm_bag)
```

**Observation:** The bagged ensemble of `nbagg = 25` decision trees achieves an OOB error rate of `r oob_bag`% on the training set and a test-set F1 of `r f1_bag`%, Recall = `r recall_bag`%, Precision = `r prec_bag`%, Accuracy = `r acc_bag`%.

**Interpretation:** Bagging reduces the high variance of a single decision tree by averaging across 25 trees trained on different bootstrap samples. The explicit 80/20 split within the balanced training data serves as an internal validation set — it confirms performance before the final held-out test set is ever consulted, mirroring the same leakage-prevention discipline applied throughout the project. Each tree sees approximately 63% of the 80% bag_train subset; the remaining 37% (out-of-bag) provides an additional, free-of-charge error estimate without touching either the validation or test sets. Comparing the bagged tree to the single decision tree (Model B) quantifies how much variance reduction bagging achieves for this dataset. Unlike the Random Forest (which also randomizes the feature split at each node), bagging uses all features at every split, making it a purer test of the variance-reduction effect of bootstrap aggregation alone.

---

# Heterogeneous Ensembles: Majority Vote and Out-of-Fold Stacking

A heterogeneous ensemble combines predictions from **different** model families — logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest. Two versions are built: a **majority vote** (this section), and a genuine **stacked** ensemble whose meta-learner is trained on out-of-fold predictions (section 24.2). *Revision note:* the earlier version called the majority vote "stacking"; stacking requires a meta-learner fit on predictions the base models made for data they were not trained on. This is distinct from bagging (which uses one model type) because it exploits the complementary strengths of each learner: the linear model captures global trends, the decision tree captures sharp nonlinear rules, and the random forest reduces variance through its own internal aggregation.

The ensemble function is defined to accept a named list of trained models and a new data frame, and returns a factor prediction based on majority vote across all three base models. This is the required interface: `function(models, data)`.

```{r ensemble-function}
# Heterogeneous stacked ensemble as a reusable function (Module 09)
# Arguments:
#   models  -- named list of caret/rpart/randomForest model objects
#   newdata -- data frame of new observations to predict
# Returns:
#   factor with levels c("Concordant", "Conflicting")

ensemble_predict <- function(models, newdata) {
  # Collect one prediction vector per model
  preds <- lapply(models, function(m) {
    if (inherits(m, "rpart")) {
      as.character(predict(m, newdata = newdata, type = "class"))
    } else {
      as.character(predict(m, newdata = newdata))
    }
  })

  # Majority vote: count "Conflicting" votes across models
  vote_mat  <- do.call(cbind, preds)           # matrix: rows = obs, cols = models
  n_models  <- ncol(vote_mat)
  conf_votes <- rowSums(vote_mat == "Conflicting")

  # Majority: strictly more than half the models vote Conflicting
  result <- ifelse(conf_votes > n_models / 2, "Conflicting", "Concordant")
  factor(result, levels = c("Concordant", "Conflicting"))
}

cat("ensemble_predict() defined.\n")
cat("Signature: ensemble_predict(models = list(...), newdata = data.frame(...))\n")
cat("Rule: majority vote -- predict Conflicting when > 50% of models agree.\n")
```

```{r ensemble-apply}
# Apply the ensemble function to the test set using all three base models
model_list  <- list(glm  = model_glm,
                    tree = model_tree,
                    rf   = model_rf)

ensemble_pred <- ensemble_predict(models = model_list, newdata = test)

cat("=== Heterogeneous Stacked Ensemble (Majority Vote) ===\n")
cat("Models combined: Logistic Regression + Decision Tree + Random Forest\n\n")
print(table(ensemble_pred))

agree_all <- sum(
  as.character(pred_glm) == as.character(pred_tree) &
  as.character(pred_tree) == as.character(pred_rf)
)
cat("\nAll three models agreed on:", agree_all, "out of", nrow(test), "cases\n")
cat("Disagreement cases resolved by majority vote.\n")
```

```{r eval-ensemble}
cm_ens     <- confusionMatrix(ensemble_pred, test$CLASS, positive = "Conflicting")
acc_ens    <- round(cm_ens$overall["Accuracy"]  * 100, 2)
f1_ens     <- round(cm_ens$byClass["F1"]         * 100, 2)
recall_ens <- round(cm_ens$byClass["Recall"]     * 100, 2)
prec_ens   <- round(cm_ens$byClass["Precision"]  * 100, 2)
cat("=== Ensemble Confusion Matrix ===\n")
print(cm_ens)
```

**Observation:** The heterogeneous stacked ensemble achieves Accuracy = `r acc_ens`%, Recall = `r recall_ens`%, Precision = `r prec_ens`%, F1 = `r f1_ens`%.

**Interpretation:** Majority vote across three diverse model families reduces the risk of any single model's systematic errors dominating the final prediction. Where all three agree, the prediction is most certain. Where two of three agree, the majority rules. The function interface (`ensemble_predict(models, newdata)`) makes the ensemble reusable on any new data frame that shares the same feature schema — it is not hard-coded to specific predictions but dispatches to each model's native `predict` method.

---

## Stacked Ensemble (Out-of-Fold Meta-Learner)

Stacking trains a **meta-learner** on the base models' predictions. To avoid leakage, those predictions must be **out-of-fold**: each tuning row's probability comes from the cross-validation fold in which that row was held out. All three base models were tuned on the same folds, so their out-of-fold probabilities line up row by row. A logistic regression on the three probabilities learns how to weight the models. On the test set it is applied to the base models' predictions for data none of them saw.

```{r stacking}
oof <- function(m, name) {
  p <- m$pred
  if (!is.null(m$bestTune) && ncol(m$bestTune) > 0)
    for (k in names(m$bestTune)) p <- p[p[[k]] == m$bestTune[[k]], ]
  p <- p[order(p$rowIndex), c("rowIndex", "obs", "Conflicting")]
  names(p)[3] <- name
  p
}
meta_train <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = c("rowIndex", "obs")),
                     list(oof(model_glm, "p_glm"), oof(tree_tuned, "p_tree"), oof(rf_tuned, "p_rf")))
stopifnot(nrow(meta_train) == length(tune_idx))
meta_model <- glm(I(obs == "Conflicting") ~ p_glm + p_tree + p_rf,
                  data = meta_train, family = binomial)
print(round(coef(summary(meta_model)), 3))

meta_test <- data.frame(
  p_glm  = predict(model_glm,  newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"],
  p_tree = predict(tree_tuned, newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"],
  p_rf   = predict(rf_tuned,   newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"]
)
prob_stack <- predict(meta_model, newdata = meta_test, type = "response")

# The meta-learner is fit at the real class balance, so 0.5 is not a sensible cut-off.
# The threshold that maximises F1 is chosen on the out-of-fold (training) predictions only.
f1_at <- function(p, y, t) { pr <- p >= t; tp <- sum(pr & y); if (tp == 0) return(0)
  2 * tp / (2 * tp + sum(pr & !y) + sum(!pr & y)) }
oof_fit   <- fitted(meta_model)
grid_t    <- seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.01)
stack_thr <- grid_t[which.max(sapply(grid_t, f1_at, p = oof_fit, y = meta_train$obs == "Conflicting"))]
pred_stack <- factor(ifelse(prob_stack >= stack_thr, "Conflicting", "Concordant"),
                     levels = c("Concordant", "Conflicting"))
cm_stack     <- confusionMatrix(pred_stack, test$CLASS, positive = "Conflicting")
acc_stack    <- round(cm_stack$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 2)
f1_stack     <- round(cm_stack$byClass["F1"]        * 100, 2)
recall_stack <- round(cm_stack$byClass["Recall"]    * 100, 2)
prec_stack   <- round(cm_stack$byClass["Precision"] * 100, 2)
auc_stack    <- auc_trap(roc_points(prob_stack, actual, "Conflicting"))
cat("Stacked ensemble -- threshold (chosen on out-of-fold data):", stack_thr,
    "| test AUC:", auc_stack, "| test F1:", f1_stack, "%\n")
```

**Observation:** The meta-learner's coefficients show how much each base model's probability contributes. On the test set the stacked ensemble reaches AUC `r auc_stack` and F1 `r f1_stack`% at a threshold of `r stack_thr`, which was chosen on out-of-fold training predictions.

**Interpretation:** Unlike the majority vote, stacking can down-weight a weaker model and use the full probability rather than a hard vote. If it does not beat the best single model, the base models are making largely the same errors.

---

## Full Performance Comparison

AUC and AUPRC are threshold-free and are the primary comparison. AUPRC (average precision) should be read against the prevalence of Conflicting variants in the test set, `r round(mean(test$CLASS == "Conflicting"), 3)`, which is what a random ranking would score. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 depend on the 0.5 cut-off (or the stacking cut-off), and accuracy must be compared with the `r round(100 * mean(test$CLASS == "Concordant"), 1)`% obtained by always predicting Concordant.

```{r full-comparison}
auprc <- function(prob, y) {                 # average precision
  o <- order(prob, decreasing = TRUE); y <- y[o]
  sum((cumsum(y) / seq_along(y))[y]) / sum(y)
}
y_test   <- test$CLASS == "Conflicting"
prob_bag <- predict(model_bag, newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "Conflicting"]
auc_bag  <- auc_trap(roc_points(prob_bag, actual, "Conflicting"))
all_results <- data.frame(
  Model         = c("A: Logistic Reg", "B: Decision Tree",
                    "C: Random Forest", "Bagged Tree (Homogeneous)",
                    "Ensemble (Majority Vote)", "Stacked Ensemble (OOF meta-learner)"),
  AUC           = round(c(auc_glm, auc_tree, auc_rf, auc_bag, NA, auc_stack), 4),
  AUPRC         = round(c(auprc(prob_glm, y_test), auprc(prob_tree, y_test), auprc(prob_rf, y_test),
                          auprc(prob_bag, y_test), NA, auprc(prob_stack, y_test)), 4),
  Accuracy_pct  = c(acc_lr,    acc_tree,   acc_rf,   acc_bag,   acc_ens,   acc_stack),
  Precision_pct = c(prec_lr,   prec_tree,  prec_rf,  prec_bag,  prec_ens,  prec_stack),
  Recall_pct    = c(recall_lr, recall_tree, recall_rf, recall_bag, recall_ens, recall_stack),
  F1_pct        = c(f1_lr,     f1_tree,    f1_rf,    f1_bag,    f1_ens,    f1_stack)
)

cat("=== Full Model Comparison (test set; percentages for threshold metrics) ===\n")
print(all_results)

# Model selection uses cross-validated AUC, never test-set performance.
best_indiv_idx  <- which.max(cv_aucs)
best_indiv_f1   <- all_results$F1_pct[best_indiv_idx]
best_indiv_name <- all_results$Model[best_indiv_idx]
improvement_pp  <- round(f1_ens - best_indiv_f1, 2)
bag_vs_tree     <- round(f1_bag - f1_tree, 2)

cat("\nBest individual model by CV AUC:", best_indiv_name, "| test F1 =", best_indiv_f1, "%\n")
cat("Bagged Tree F1        :", f1_bag, "% (vs single tree:", f1_tree, "%,",
    bag_vs_tree, "pp change)\n")
cat("Ensemble F1           :", f1_ens, "%\n")
cat("Improvement (Ens vs best indiv):", improvement_pp, "percentage points\n")
```

```{r final-barplot}
bar_colors <- c("#90CAF9", "#90CAF9", "#90CAF9", "#FFB74D", "#F44336", "#7E57C2")

barplot(all_results$F1_pct,
        names.arg = c("A: LR", "B: Tree", "C: RF", "Bagged", "Vote", "Stacked"),
        col  = bar_colors, ylim = c(0, 100), las = 2,
        main = "F1-Score (%) -- All Models (test set)",
        ylab = "F1 Score (%)")
abline(h = best_indiv_f1, lty = 2, col = "navy")
legend("topright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Individual models",
                  "Bagged (homogeneous)",
                  "Ensemble (majority vote)",
                  "Stacked (out-of-fold)",
                  paste("F1 of best-by-CV model:", best_indiv_f1, "%")),
       fill = c("#90CAF9", "#FFB74D", "#F44336", "#7E57C2", NA),
       lty  = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, 2),
       col  = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, "navy"))
```

**Observation:** The ensemble achieves an F1 of `r f1_ens`%, which is `r improvement_pp` percentage points `r ifelse(improvement_pp >= 0, "above", "below")` the best individual model (`r best_indiv_name` at `r best_indiv_f1`%). The bagged tree achieves F1 = `r f1_bag`% vs. the single Decision Tree at `r f1_tree`% (`r bag_vs_tree` pp change). Ensemble Accuracy = `r acc_ens`%, Recall = `r recall_ens`%, Precision = `r prec_ens`%.

**Interpretation:** The bagged tree isolates the variance-reduction effect of bootstrap aggregation: by training 25 trees on different bootstrap samples of the same training set, variance is reduced without changing the model family. The heterogeneous ensemble goes further by combining three completely different model families, exploiting the fact that logistic regression, decision trees, and random forests make different kinds of errors. Where the two ensembles improve over the best individual model, that improvement comes from error cancellation across diverse learners.

# Applying the Ensemble to Example Records

The reusable `ensemble_predict()` function is demonstrated on five records drawn from the held-out test set. They are unseen by every model, but they are **not new data**: they are already counted in the test metrics above and are shown only to illustrate how the function is called and how the models vote.

```{r final-prediction}
set.seed(999)
conc_idx  <- sample(which(test$CLASS == "Concordant"),  3)
conf_idx  <- sample(which(test$CLASS == "Conflicting"), 2)
new_obs   <- test[c(conc_idx, conf_idx), ]

# Apply the reusable ensemble function to five held-out example records
new_ens   <- ensemble_predict(models = model_list, newdata = new_obs)

new_tree  <- as.character(
  predict(model_tree, newdata = new_obs, type = "class")
)
new_rf    <- as.character(predict(model_rf,  newdata = new_obs))
new_glm   <- as.character(predict(model_glm, newdata = new_obs))
new_bag   <- as.character(predict(model_bag, newdata = new_obs))

pred_table <- data.frame(
  Sample    = 1:5,
  Actual    = as.character(new_obs$CLASS),
  GLM_Pred  = new_glm,
  Tree_Pred = new_tree,
  RF_Pred   = new_rf,
  Bag_Pred  = new_bag,
  Ensemble  = as.character(new_ens),
  Correct   = as.character(new_obs$CLASS) == as.character(new_ens)
)

print(pred_table)
n_correct_ens <- sum(pred_table$Correct)
n_all_agree   <- sum(new_tree == new_rf & new_rf == new_glm)

cat("\nEnsemble correct:", n_correct_ens, "out of 5\n")
cat("All three base models agreed:", n_all_agree, "out of 5 cases\n")
```

**Observation:** The ensemble correctly classified `r n_correct_ens` of the 5 example records (an illustration, not an accuracy estimate). In `r n_all_agree` cases all three base models agreed on the prediction.

**Interpretation:** The `ensemble_predict()` function applies each model's native `predict` method to new data and resolves disagreements by majority vote. Cases where all three models agree are the highest-confidence predictions. The bagged tree column additionally shows how a homogeneous ensemble of 25 trees handles the same observations.

# Gene-Grouped Cross-Validation Check

With a random split, variants of the same gene can sit in both the training and the test data. A model can then score well by learning which **genes** tend to have conflicting interpretations rather than which **variant properties** predict conflict. Gene identity was never a feature here (`SYMBOL` was dropped), but correlated fields can stand in for it, for example genomic position (`POS` is a feature in this pipeline: `r "POS" %in% features`).

To measure this, the random forest is cross-validated twice on the same stratified 15,000-variant subsample of the original training set, with the same settings and upsampling inside each training fold:

- **random 5-fold**: variants are assigned to folds at random;
- **gene-grouped 5-fold** (`caret::groupKFold`): all variants of a gene are kept in the same fold, so every validation fold contains only genes the model has not seen.

```{r gene-grouped}
set.seed(555)
gg_idx  <- createDataPartition(train_cv$CLASS, p = min(1, 15000 / nrow(train_cv)), list = FALSE)[, 1]
gg_data <- train_cv[gg_idx, ]
gg_gene <- train_gene[gg_idx]
set.seed(556)
rand_folds <- createFolds(gg_data$CLASS, k = 5, returnTrain = TRUE)
gene_folds <- groupKFold(gg_gene, k = 5)

run_grouped_cv <- function(folds) {
  ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", index = folds, sampling = "up", classProbs = TRUE,
                       summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)
  set.seed(557)
  m <- train(CLASS ~ ., data = gg_data, method = "rf", metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
             tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = best_mtry), ntree = 100)
  c(CV_AUC = m$results$ROC, AUC_SD_across_folds = m$results$ROCSD)
}
gg_res <- rbind(`Random 5-fold`       = run_grouped_cv(rand_folds),
                `Gene-grouped 5-fold` = run_grouped_cv(gene_folds))
n_genes_gg <- length(unique(gg_gene))
print(round(gg_res, 4))
gg_drop <- round(gg_res[1, 1] - gg_res[2, 1], 4)
cat("Variants:", nrow(gg_data), "| genes:", n_genes_gg, "| AUC drop when genes are held out:", gg_drop, "\n")
```

**Observation:** On `r nrow(gg_data)` variants from `r n_genes_gg` genes, the random forest's cross-validated AUC is `r round(gg_res[1, 1], 3)` with random folds and `r round(gg_res[2, 1], 3)` when whole genes are held out (a difference of `r gg_drop`).

**Interpretation:** The gene-grouped AUC is the better estimate of performance on variants in genes absent from the training data. Any gap between the two numbers is the part of the random-split performance that comes from recognising genes rather than variant properties. The random-split test-set metrics reported above should be read with that in mind.

---

# Conclusion

This project built a complete CRISP-DM machine learning pipeline to predict conflicting ClinVar variant classifications using `r nrow(df)` records from Kaggle. All preprocessing decisions were derived from the training set and applied identically to the test set, and cross-validation upsamples inside each training fold, so neither the test set nor the validation folds leak into training.

`r length(drop_all)` columns were removed for near-complete missingness or high cardinality. Random-forest imputation models, fitted on the training set only, filled missing values in `r length(num_miss_cols)` numeric and `r length(char_miss_cols)` integer-encoded character columns, and the same models filled the test set. IQR-based outlier capping replaced `r format(total_capped, big.mark = ",")` extreme values (training and test combined) with the training-set fence values. The `log1p` transformation was applied to the three allele frequency columns because they showed right-skewed distributions. Two engineered features — `avg_AF` and `is_rare_variant` — summarized allele frequency information. The rarity threshold was derived from the 25th percentile of non-zero training values to guarantee a non-constant feature.

Chi-square tests on `r length(int_cols)` low-cardinality features found `r n_sig` statistically significant marginal associations at p < 0.05. PCA showed `r n_80` components explain 80% of variance, with `r top_pc1_feature` driving PC1. K-means clustering with K = 3 found clusters that contain mixed classes, indicating weak natural separation and confirming that supervised models are necessary.

| Model | CV AUC | Test AUC | Test AUPRC | Accuracy | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: Logistic Reg | `r best_glm_cv` | `r all_results$AUC[1]` | `r all_results$AUPRC[1]` | `r acc_lr`% | `r prec_lr`% | `r recall_lr`% | `r f1_lr`% |
| B: Decision Tree | `r best_tree_auc` | `r all_results$AUC[2]` | `r all_results$AUPRC[2]` | `r acc_tree`% | `r prec_tree`% | `r recall_tree`% | `r f1_tree`% |
| C: Random Forest | `r best_rf_auc` | `r all_results$AUC[3]` | `r all_results$AUPRC[3]` | `r acc_rf`% | `r prec_rf`% | `r recall_rf`% | `r f1_rf`% |
| Bagged Tree (Homogeneous) | — | `r all_results$AUC[4]` | `r all_results$AUPRC[4]` | `r acc_bag`% | `r prec_bag`% | `r recall_bag`% | `r f1_bag`% |
| Ensemble (Majority Vote) | — | — | — | `r acc_ens`% | `r prec_ens`% | `r recall_ens`% | `r f1_ens`% |
| Stacked Ensemble (OOF) | — | `r all_results$AUC[6]` | `r all_results$AUPRC[6]` | `r acc_stack`% | `r prec_stack`% | `r recall_stack`% | `r f1_stack`% |

The model with the best cross-validated AUC is `r best_indiv_name` (test F1 `r best_indiv_f1`%); model choice uses cross-validation, and the test set is used only to report performance. AUPRC should be compared with the `r round(mean(test$CLASS == "Conflicting"), 3)` prevalence of Conflicting variants, and accuracy with the `r round(100 * mean(test$CLASS == "Concordant"), 1)`% of always predicting Concordant: every model's accuracy is below that baseline because the models were trained on balanced classes and use a 0.5 cut-off, which trades accuracy for recall. Discrimination is modest (test AUC `r sprintf("%.3f", min(all_results$AUC, na.rm = TRUE))`–`r sprintf("%.3f", max(all_results$AUC, na.rm = TRUE))`), and the gene-grouped check estimates how much of it depends on recognising genes seen in training (random-fold CV AUC `r round(gg_res[1, 1], 3)` vs gene-grouped `r round(gg_res[2, 1], 3)`). The majority-vote ensemble changed F1 by `r improvement_pp` percentage points relative to the best-by-CV model. The bagged tree (`r f1_bag`% F1) compared to the single Decision Tree (`r f1_tree`% F1) shows a `r bag_vs_tree` pp change from bootstrap aggregation alone. The Random Forest is itself a form of bagging with additional feature randomization, which is why it achieves higher precision than the plain bagged tree despite both using decision trees internally. Logistic regression provides an interpretable linear baseline but is limited by the nonlinear structure of genomic data. The `ensemble_predict()` function provides a reusable interface that can be applied to any new data frame sharing the same feature schema.

Clustering failed to cleanly separate the classes because the Concordant and Conflicting variants overlap substantially in the feature space — both classes exist in every cluster. This confirms that the class boundary is not a simple distance-based separation in the original feature space, and supervised learning is required to detect it.

If missing a truly conflicting variant were costlier than a false alarm, a high-recall operating point would be preferred: at the cut-offs used here the highest recall is `r all_results$Model[which.max(all_results$Recall_pct)]` at `r max(all_results$Recall_pct)`%. Recall depends on the chosen threshold, though, and with test AUCs of at most `r sprintf("%.3f", max(all_results$AUC, na.rm = TRUE))` none of these models is suitable for clinical use; this is a methods demonstration.

**Limitations:**

- PolyPhen and SIFT were over 60% missing. Random-forest imputation estimates these from other annotations rather than measuring them, so more complete functional annotation would likely improve all models.
- ClinVar interpretations change over time, and "conflicting" partly reflects how many laboratories submitted a variant, which is not a biological property of the variant itself.
- A single random train–test split is used, so variants of the same gene appear in both sets; the gene-grouped check above estimates the effect of that.
